source_text: Jam vero si ex mortuis vivi, utique singuli ex singulis. Singulorum ergo corporum animas, ut singulas in singula corpora reverti oportuerat. Porro si et binae et trinae et quinae usque uno utero resumuntur, non erunt ex mortuis vivi, quia non singuli ex singulis. Et hoc autem modo primordii forma singulatur, cum et nunc plures animae de una proferuntur. Item, cum varia aetate decedant animae, cur una revertuntur? omnes enim ab infantia imbuuntur. Quale est autem ut senex defunctus, infans revertatur? si decrescit foris anima retrograda aetate, quanto magis erat ut progressior reverteretur mille post annis? Certe vel coaetanea suae mortis, ut aevum quod reliquisset, iterum recepisset. Sed etsi eaedem semper revolverentur, licet non corporum quoque formas easdem, tamen vel ingeniorum et studiorum et adfectionum pristinas proprietates secum referre deberent; quoniam temere eaedem haberentur, carentes iis per quae eaedem probarentur. Unde scias, inquis, an ita quidem fiat occulte, sed conditio milliarii aevi interimat facultatem recensendi, quia ignotae tibi revertuntur? Atquin scio non ita fieri, cum Pythagoram, Euphorbum mihi opponis. Ecce enim Euphorbum militarem et bellicam animam satis constat vel de ipsa gloria clypeorum consecratorum; Pythagoram vero tam residem et imbellem, ut praelia tunc Graeciae vitans, Italiae maluerit quietem, geometricae et astrologiae et musicae devotus, alienus studio et adfectu Euphorbi. Sed et Pyrrhus ille fallendis piscibus agebat; Pythagoras contra nec edendis, ut animalibus abstinens. Aethalides autem et Hermotimus fabam quoque in pabulis communibus inruerat; Pythagoras vero ne per fabalia quidem transeundum discipulis suis tradidit. Quomodo ergo eaedem animae recuperantur, quae nec ingeniis, nec institutis jam, nec victibus eaedem probabuntur? Jam nunc, de tanto Graeciae censu quatuor solae animae recensentur. Sed et quid utique de solo Graeciae censu, ut non ex omni gente, ex omni aetate ac dignitate, ex omni denique sexu, et μετεμψυχώσεις μετενσωματώσεις quotidie existant, cur solus Pythagoras alium atque alium se recognoscat, non et ego? aut si privilegium philosophorum est, et utique graecorum, quasi non et scythae et indi philosophentur, cur neminem se retro meminit Epicurus, neminem Chrysippus, neminem Zeno, ne ipse quidem Plato, quem forsitan Nestorem credidissemus, ob mella facundiae?
pass_a_gloss: But indeed if from the dead the living come, certainly single ones from single ones. Therefore, the souls of single bodies ought to return as single ones into single bodies. Furthermore, if also twofold and threefold and fivefold ones are taken back into one womb, they will not be from the dead the living, because not single ones from single ones. And in this manner, the form of the beginning is made single, when now also multiple souls are brought forth from one. Likewise, when souls pass away at various ages, why do they return as one? For all are imbued from infancy. What kind is it, then, that when an old man has died, an infant returns? If the soul decreases outwardly with retrograde age, how much more was it that it should return as more advanced a thousand years later? Certainly, at least, it should have received again the age which it had left, as a coeval of its own death. But even if the same souls were always being turned back, although not also the same forms of bodies, nevertheless, they ought to bring back with them the former properties of characters and studies and affections; since they would be considered the same without those things by which they would be proven the same. Whence do you know, you ask, whether it happens in this way secretly, but the condition of the age prevents the faculty of recognizing, because unknown ones return to you? But I know it does not happen in this way, since you oppose to me Pythagoras and Euphorbus. For Euphorbus, a military and warlike soul, is well known, even from the glory of the consecrated shields; Pythagoras, indeed, so resident and unwarlike, that, avoiding the battles of Greece at that time, he preferred the quiet of Italy, devoted to geometry and astrology and music, alien to the study and affection of Euphorbus. But also that Pyrrhus was busy deceiving fish; Pythagoras, on the other hand, not even eating them, as one abstaining from animals. Aethalides and Hermotimus, however, also rushed into the common food of beans; Pythagoras, indeed, handed down to his disciples that they should not even pass through the bean fields. How, therefore, are the same souls recovered, which will not be proven the same by characters, or by institutions, or by food? Now, from so great a census of Greece, only four souls are reckoned. But also, what certainly about the census of Greece alone, so that not from every nation, from every age and dignity, from every sex, and metempsychoses and transmigrations exist daily, why does only Pythagoras recognize another and another as himself, and not I? Or if it is a privilege of philosophers, and certainly of Greeks, as if not also Scythians and Indians philosophize, why does Epicurus not remember himself backward, nor Chrysippus, nor Zeno, nor even Plato himself, whom we might have believed to be Nestor, on account of the honey of eloquence?
pass_b_english: If the living come from the dead, they must come one-to-one. That means each individual soul ought to return to its own individual body. But if two, three, or five souls are crammed back into a single womb, the living are no longer coming from the dead, because the one-to-one rule is broken. This whole theory forces the primordial pattern into a singleton mold, even though right now multiple souls are born from one mother. Then there is the age problem: souls die at every stage of life, so why do they all come back as infants? Everyone starts from infancy. What sense does it make for an old man to die and return as a baby? If the soul shrinks outward with age going in reverse, it should have been even more fitting for it to come back more advanced a thousand years later. At minimum, it should have retrieved the exact age it left, returning as a contemporary of its own death.

Even granting that the same souls recycle, they ought to carry their old character traits, pursuits, and passions with them, even if their bodies change. Without those markers, they would be declared the same arbitrarily, lacking the very evidence that would prove identity. You ask how I know this does not happen secretly, since the sheer length of time destroys the ability to recognize returning strangers? I know it does not happen, and Exhibit A is your own star witness: Pythagoras and Euphorbus. Euphorbus was a military, warlike soul, well attested by the fame of his dedicated shields. Pythagoras, by contrast, was so sedentary and unwarlike that he fled the wars of Greece for the quiet of Italy, devoting himself to geometry, astrology, and music, utterly alien to Euphorbus' pursuits and passions. Then there is Pyrrhus, who made a practice of tricking fish; Pythagoras would not even eat them, abstaining from animals. Aethalides and Hermotimus dove into common fare like beans; Pythagoras forbade his disciples even to walk through bean fields. How can the same souls be recovered when they fail to match in character, in training, or in diet?

Right now, out of the vast population of Greece, only four souls are claimed to have recycled. But why stop at Greece? If metempsychosis and transmigration happen daily across every nation, every age, every rank, and both sexes, why does only Pythagoras recognize his past selves, and not me? If this is a philosophers' privilege, and a Greek one at that, as if Scythians and Indians do not philosophize, why do Epicurus, Chrysippus, Zeno, and even Plato himself recall nothing? We might have believed Plato was Nestor reincarnated, given the honey of his eloquence.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex arguments regarding the individuality of souls and the contradictions in the theory of metempsychosis. Pass A provides a faithful literal translation, and Pass B provides a fluent, accurate rendering that preserves all nuances, including the specific examples of Pythagoras, Euphorbus, and the dietary habits of the disciples. All Greek terms (μετεμψυχώσεις μετενσωματώσεις) are correctly handled. The title 'Resurrection of Souls' is a suitable thematic description of the thought expressed in the locus.

The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the argumentation, logical structure, and key terms. The inline citations are correctly applied where relevant. The title 'Resurrection of Souls' appropriately captures the central theme of the passage. The translation maintains the author's distinctions regarding agency, modality, and doctrine. No errors in source identity, completeness, or fidelity to the original text are detected.
